he should produce a sweet sound from the drums and other instruments for three beats;
then the Vajra-holder should recite the song, and thereafter begin the *tāṇḍava* dance.
The one who corrupts the five masters and four goddesses is indeed of the nature of Acalā;
in the place of the maṇḍala hall, he should perform the Buddha-dance.

The sequence for this [verse] from the *Ḍākinīvajrapañjara* (2.59) is written as follows: Thereafter, one should produce pleasant sounds such as drums and *tīṇaśaṅkha* shells. Then, singing songs of equanimity, that Vajra-holder should commence the dance. Abiding firmly within the maṇḍala house, together with the five masters and the four goddesses—the very self of Acala and the jokers—one should perform the dance, the dramatic performance of the Buddhas. Following this, the sequence should be written down.

In that regard, in a place such as a mandala house that has been prepared according to the rules, provided with song and instrumental music, and supplied with the requisites for the mandala and various kinds of food and drink, the Vajrin—who possesses the yoga of the mandala to be drawn—should not admit anyone who is not a disciple out of fear of violating the samaya. According to this statement, since there is no [other] disciple of one's own, other disciples may also be admitted after having them undergo the preliminary consecration (*adhivāsana*) ritual, preceded by the recitation of the injunction for bestowing the Vajradhara vows.

One should perform the ritual exactly as prescribed: in a mandala house or similar location, properly equipped with songs, music, and so forth, as well as all that is required for the mandala, such as food and drink. Then, the Vajra-holder endowed with the yoga of the mandala—fearing that the samaya might be violated—[should proceed].

Because of the statement, "One should not initiate those who are not one's own disciples," even if one has no disciples of one's own, one should initiate the disciples of others as well, having first performed the preliminary request and the *adhivāsana* (formal acceptance), and having bestowed the Vajradhara vows.

Likewise, there are four disciples, each possessing the yoga of their respective Universal Monarchs (cakravartin). Similarly, there are four yoginīs who, having assumed the status of maṇḍala-deities of their respective Universal Monarchs, are actually males in the form of women, joined with a retinue of women. Furthermore, there is another, Acala, who is intent upon subduing all Māras.

Thus, the four disciples, each possessing their own universal monarch yoga, and likewise the four yoginīs, each fully visualizing their own universal monarch mandala; and in the absence of a woman, even a man is perfectly endowed with the attire and characteristics of a woman;
and likewise, the immovable ones are the supreme subduers of all Māras.

There, in the northeast of the mandala—or in another direction where there is no space—behind a curtain, [the practitioner], whose body has the color of ink and so forth, with a face corresponding to his own deity; with a blazing gaze produced by the syllable *HŪṂ*; with eyes contracted by the knitting of brows in great wrath;

and with flames of gaze as difficult to endure as the fire at the end of an aeon, having driven away the Māras, acts as a Vajradhara assuming a fabricated form, black in color, situated in the center, in order to establish all sentient beings in the great bliss that is the single flavor of non-dual suchness.

Alternatively, from another direction of the mandala's sovereign boundary, within the curtain, one should smear one's face and body with colors such as black pigment to match the respective color of each deity.

From the syllable *hūṃ*, [he becomes] one with blazing eyeballs, a great wrathful deity with a furrowed brow and eyes of shifting expression; with a gaze like the fire at the end of the eon that is difficult to endure, he shall expel the māras.
In the center is the black Vajradhara, the possessor of the vajra, who acts for the sake of establishing all sentient beings in the great bliss that is of one taste with non-dual suchness.

Likewise, at the eastern gate stands the white, eternal Kṛtrimacakradhara, who—like Mount Sumeru—is steadfast, and who, with a gaze of loving-kindness and unblinking eyes, and with a garland of cool, white rays transformed by the syllable Oṃ and Tārī, establishes those who have perished from [wrong] views and those who observe the vows of nihilists within the delusion of the Buddha in non-abiding nirvāṇa.

Likewise, with eyes as stable and immovable as Mount Meru, possessing a gaze of loving-kindness, and with pupils formed from the syllable *oṃ*, he emitted garlands of white light rays of cooling nectar; for the sake of establishing those who were destitute of excellence and those who maintained vows of non-existence within the Buddha’s non-abiding nirvāṇa beyond delusion, he acted thus.
The white eternal one (nitya) holding a wheel is at the eastern gate.

Likewise, at the western gate is Narteśvara, red in color with the hue of passion, holding a conventional lotus; he is positioned there with a gaze directed toward the left side of the one resting on his left, using the hook of light-rays from the syllable Hrīḥ as Tārā to establish Śrāvakas and others—who are inclined toward the transformation of awakening—within the state of Great Passion (mahārāga).

Likewise, at the western gate is the Lord of the Dance, who holds a lotus and is red in color with an expression of passion; he is intended to establish the Śrāvakas and others—who rely on the left, follow the left, and possess views originating from the syllable *hrīḥ*, whose eye-sockets are formed by light-rays like iron hooks, and who are to be transformed into perfect enlightenment—within the awakening of great passion.

Likewise, at the northern gate, [the deity] holding a sword made of jewels or having a body of a crossed-vajra (viśvavajra), with a blue supreme horse, acts as one who holds a non-artificial sword; by means of a blazing gaze formed from the syllable *khaṃ* and a hook, and by relying on the path of the Omniscient One, he brings even those who have reached the stages of a Bodhisattva—through the display of accomplishments—as well as those who have entered the paths of the Śrāvakas and others, to certainty in perfect enlightenment by displaying various emanations.

Likewise, just as the syllable *khaṃ* forms the eyeballs, those who see the siddhi of attaining the bodhisattva stages by relying on the path of omniscience through the blazing iron hook [of wisdom], and—

At the northern gate is the green horse-king holding a sword, intended for the purpose of establishing those who see various forms of nirvāṇa through faith in the paths of the śrāvakas and so forth in perfect and complete enlightenment.

Likewise, at the southern gate is the yellow Vajrasūrya, who holds artificial jewels; he is seated upon a yellow moon born from the syllable *jaḥ*, and with an upward gaze fixed on a goad, he removes the envy of those corrupted by pride and establishes them in the wisdom of equanimity.

Likewise, from the syllable *ja*, there arises a yellow iron hook (*aṅkuśa*) held in the right hand and gazing upward; this yellow Vajra-Sun holding a jewel is placed at the southern gate in order to render arrogant and malevolent beings free from stinginess and to firmly establish them in the wisdom of equality (*samatājñāna*).
This is because of the statement: "East, west, north, and south.
(From the *Ḍākinīvajrapañjara* 14.114).
This is because of the statement: "In the eastern, western, northern, and southern directions."

They wear their sacred threads over the right shoulder (apasavya) like those performing a sacrifice; they carry skull-topped staffs (khaṭvāṅga), hold vajras and bells, or carry skulls in their hands. All of them are clothed in tiger skins and adorned with ornaments made of human bone. Their hair is artificially dyed tawny and tied upward; they wear garlands of skulls and crowns representing the five Buddhas. They perform the *tāṇḍava* dance in the half-lotus posture (*ardhaparyaṅka*), or stand in the *ālīḍha* stance. They have three eyes and stand upon artificial double-lotuses and sun disks. Śāśvata, however, sits upon a lotus and moon seat and possesses the radiance of the moon.
All of these hold in their left hands objects for making offerings, such as a *khatvāṅga*, a vajra bell, or a *kapāla*.

Wearing a lower garment made of tiger skin, adorned with human bones and the like, with yellow hair tied upward, and bearing a garland of skulls and a crown of the five Buddhas; he stands in the half-lotus posture (*ardhaparyaṅka*) or in the dancing pose with the right leg extended, possessing three eyes, and resting upon a variegated lotus and sun disk—though the permanent [deities] rest upon a lotus and moon, being endowed with their radiance.

In the same way, in the northeast corner is the white Locanā, who holds a wheel and pacifies the afflictions of sentient beings through her gaze of loving-kindness; [however], in the Hevajra maṇḍala, she is in another location, the southeast corner.
In the same way, with a compassionate gaze, having eliminated harm to others, the blue Māmakī, whose hands hold a fabricated vajra and lotus,
is in the southeast corner.

In the same way, in the south-western corner (Nairṛtya), there is the red Pāṇḍarā, who, holding an artificial lotus, impassions people with her gaze that is red with passion. She is dressed in white and is red in color.
Likewise, in the northwest corner is green Tārā, who, with a gaze of attraction, draws in those to be trained;
she holds a fabricated blue lotus.

All [the goddesses] are as before, with tawny hair standing upright on their heads; they possess artificial three-eyed faces and so forth. Their left hands form the heart-mudrā and the threatening gesture (*tarjanī*); they wear artificial garments of the universe and stand upon artificial universal lotuses and suns. They perform the *tāṇḍava* dance in the half-lotus posture (*ardhaparyaṅka*) or stand in the *pratyālīḍha* stance. Their limbs are smeared with ink of their own respective colors, or they wear garments and ornaments provided by donors or whatever is available.

All of them, as before, have three eyes with yellow hair on their heads curling upward, and each possesses their respective facial features; they have the index finger of the left fist placed at the heart, wear various garments, and abide upon various lotuses and suns, either in the *ardhaparyaṅka* dance posture or standing with the left leg extended.
He possesses a sword anointed with gold that is as immovable as reality itself, as well as garments and ornaments obtained exactly as they were offered by embodied donors.

Likewise, because he is intent on gazing upon the lower and upper realms of saṃsāra and nirvāṇa, he is yellow, squint-eyed, and immovable. He holds a noose of serpents attached to his index finger. He is intent on sporting with the Cakravartin goddesses. He stands in the pratyālīḍha posture upon a sun disc on a universal lotus, or else he stands in the position of a Vidyādhara. Whirling beside each of the Cakravartin goddesses, he is adorned with various jewels and ornaments, dressed in fine garments, and wears a jeweled crown embellished by Citteśa.

Because he possesses the supreme eye that gazes downward upon saṃsāra and upward toward nirvāṇa, he is yellow and immovable; holding a snake-noose coiled around his fingers, he is the supreme one who laughs at the goddesses of the universal monarchs, standing upon a variegated lotus and the sun with his left leg extended.

Alternatively, he stands in the posture of a universal monarch (cakravartin), surrounded by the goddesses of each respective universal monarch; he is adorned with various jewels and the like, wears fine garments, and possesses a jeweled crown adorned with the Lord of the Mind (cittādhipati).
[They perform] the vajra-stances on all sides. Singing the vajra-songs in due order, they dance at the doors with the fivefold vajra-stances, such as the lotus-turn (*kamalāvarta*) and so forth.

With its wheels perfectly circular, with raised parasols, banners, and canopies,
and with the resounding music of many instruments, it was further rendered delightful by excellent songs.

Upon the mandala circle adorned with beautiful ornaments, one should raise canopies, parasols, and banners; with various musical instruments such as melodious sounds, one should thereafter perform the most excellent and heart-pleasing songs.
Behold this wondrous, divine drama, the entire world whose nature is the five Buddhas! For therein, that which is called "Great Bliss," though one, dances as many through its manifold flavors.

Having perceived all beings here as the nature of the five Buddhas, one should perform the diverse divine dance; where there is that which is called "sole great bliss," it performs the dance alone amidst the manifold hosts.
O monk, do not train in the vehicle of the śrāvakas, nor in those practices that involve wandering or staying there;
instead, practice the conduct of awakening toward the qualities of a Buddha, for this shall be the cause for you to become a self-arisen one.

The śramaṇa does not train in the vehicle of the śrāvakas; rather, he then practices there the conduct of the ultimate truth. By practicing the conduct of awakening, these qualities of a Buddha will certainly be bestowed upon him as a self-arisen one.
By that which the dull-witted are bound, the wise are liberated;
through the cultivation of awakening, all this is seen as inverted.
Whosoever is bound by delusion, upon being completely liberated from it, becomes a Buddha; one should cultivate awakening with respect to all these inversions.

After this recitation, by removing the curtain, the Vajrin emerges while sequentially revealing [the body] from the crown, forehead, eye, chin, neck, shoulders, arms, heart, navel, knees, and feet, as if dispelling the obscurations of the stages beginning with Pramuditā through such indication. Holding a handful of flowers at the heart with the Vajrasattva-mudrā, one should visualize a moon disc in both hands produced from the syllable *Aṃ*, upon which is a white vajra-flower born from the syllable *Hūṃ*, and the fingers in the form of vajras.
This is the sequence for the other vessels as well.

At the conclusion of reciting this, the veil is removed. Then, in successive order, the crown ornament, the eyes, the forehead, the throat, the shoulders, the heart, the navel, the knees, and the feet are shown. The Vajra-holder, who symbolizes the state of being free from the obscurations of the Joyous Ground (*pramuditā-bhūmi*) and so forth, should inspire [the disciple] with certainty.

Holding the flower-vase with the mudrā of Vajrasattva at the heart, one should visualize a moon mandala arising from the syllable *Oṃ* upon the hands, and within it, a white vajra-flower produced from the syllable *Hūṃ*; the fingers as well should be visualized in the form of vajras. Likewise, this is the sequence for the other principal deities.

Then, having bent into the half-lotus posture and placed the right foot in the *samapāda* stance, one should enter through the gates into the center of the maṇḍala by means of the *ālīḍha* and other postures.

Then, having drawn back into the half-lotus posture and placed the right foot in the *samapāda* stance, one should enter through the gates into the center of the maṇḍala by means of the *ālīḍha* and other movements.

Then, having assumed an even stance, one should rotate the creeper with the hand. Following that, reciting "Oṃ namas te hūṃ | Oṃ namāmi hūṃ | Oṃ namo namaḥ hūṃ svāhā," one should raise it in sequence and release it upon the head.

Following that, having gradually consumed [the offerings] with "Namaḥ huṃ oṃ namo mi huṃ oṃ namo namaḥ huṃ svāhā" and touched [the vessel] to the crown of the head, one should offer oneself by reciting:

"I prostrate to all the Tathāgatas; I surrender myself to all the Tathāgatas. Having thus surrendered oneself, one should recite the verse of auspiciousness for the leader of the maṇḍala to be drawn, while performing the appropriate gestures.

"O Protector, I offer myself to all the Tathāgatas; to all the Tathāgatas, I dedicate myself. Reciting these words, one should perform the manner of offering to the central deity of the mandala who will question [the candidate], and the verses for pronouncing auspiciousness should be recited.

Thereafter, one should recite three times: "As many beings as are included within the collection of beings—whether born from eggs, born from a womb, born from moisture, or born spontaneously; whether possessing form or formless; whether percipient, non-percipient, or neither percipient nor non-percipient—all of them must be established by me in the state of Mahāmudrā."

"Those who do not go, their heads shall be split into a hundred pieces by the blazing hundreds of rays of light from the various vajras or swords in my hand," he should say this three times with pride throughout.
There, taking recourse to the northeastern direction, one should first employ the fourfold vajra-step.

Having visualized a single-pronged vajra at the soles of one's feet from the syllable *hūṃ*, and striking the ground while reciting the *hūṃ* mantra, one should hold the vajra and bell at the waist and dance, circling to the left with the *kamalāvarta* and other movements.

Having visualized a single-pronged vajra at the soles of one's feet from the syllable *hūṃ*, and striking the ground while reciting the *hūṃ* mantra, one should circle [the space] by performing the dance or the *padakora* (lotus-turn) and so forth, holding the vajra and bell at the waist.
Thereafter,
the three-pronged [vajra] is likewise.
Thereafter,
likewise, the five-pronged [vajra].
Thereafter, likewise, the viśvavajra;
however, by turning it around and rotating it, one forms its shape.
Nevertheless, having turned back, one should circumambulate and perform the ritual forms.

These four are called "vajra-stances" (*vajrapada*) because they are marked by the vajra and take the form of the vajra. These four should be performed individually once each, circling clockwise, using the postures such as *ālīḍha* and so forth.
Furthermore, when performing the actions such as extending the right leg individually, one should do it once each time.
In that posture, having bent the left leg, one should place the right foot five *vitastis* away, gracefully and straight; this is the *ālīḍha* stance.
"Having bent the left leg, one should remain with the right leg extended in a graceful posture to a height of five cubits; this is the *pratyālīḍha* stance."
Bending the right leg and likewise the left, this is the *pratyālīḍha* stance.
"Having contracted the right leg, the left is likewise" means that the left is extended.
With the outer toes of the feet measuring twenty-six finger-widths in length,
and with both knees held rigid, this is the standing posture named Vaiśākha.
With a width of twenty-six finger-breadths, the toes of the feet pointing outward and the two knees held straight, this is the posture known as the "Vṛṣabha" (the Bull) stance.
The Vaiśākha position itself, with a distance of two cubits between the hands and shaped like the two wings of a swan, is the maṇḍala position.
The circular stance (*maṇḍala-pada*) is formed by spreading the legs two cubits apart, with the hands positioned like the wings of a swan in the *sa-ga* posture itself.
By the mutual interlacing of the toes of both feet,
it is the even stance (*samapāda*).
For each of these five acts, one should perform one complete circumambulation in a clockwise direction as a counter-act.
When performing these five [rites], one should complete each individual circumambulation once.

With a distance of four finger-breadths between the two heels, one should keep the left foot straight and place the right foot obliquely at a distance of one span (vitasti), with grace, like the stance of Tārā of Vaiśālī; this is the *jātapada* (the "born" stance).

With a distance of four fingers between the two heels, having made the left foot straight and placed the right foot obliquely at a distance of one span, with grace, standing to the side like the stance of Tārā of Vaiśālī—this is the *jātapada*.
In the same way, one should extend the right leg straight and place the left across; this is the *pratyājātapada* (the step of the reborn).
Thus, extending the right [leg] straight while the left remains sideways is the *pratyājātapada*.
Having assumed an even stance, one should place the right foot three *vitasti*s in front of the left; this is the *vikaṭapada* (the wide-striding stance).
Having assumed an even stance, holding the right foot three *vitasti*s in front of the left is the *vikṛtapada* (the distorted stance).
In the same manner, having straightened the right [leg], one should hold the left [leg] in front of the right at a distance of three *vitastis*;
this is the *prativikaṭapada* stance, known as the "alternating stride."
One should also perform the *saṃpuṭa* posture by joining the two soles of the feet together even while seated; thus, it is called the "joined" (*saṃpuṭa*) stance.
To step upon the left foot with the right foot is the *kūrmapada* (tortoise-step).
To press the instep of the left foot with the right foot is the *kūrmapada*.
Lifting one foot and circling with the other is the *ekapada* (single-step) stance.
Lifting one foot and moving about on one foot is the *ekapada* stance.

One should perform these seven steps or postures in a fixed manner. Regarding the *bhramarījāla*: it is called *bhramarījāla* because one rotates the body in both clockwise and counter-clockwise directions while grasping one's own big toes with both hands.
The "bee-web" (*bhramarajāla*) is also [a mudrā]. The "bee-step" (*bhramarapada*) consists of the fingers of both the right and left hands moving completely [outward] from their respective sides.

While performing these thirteen [postures] beginning with *ālīḍha*, one should execute, as appropriate, the four foot-placements—namely *sāgarāndola*, *parvatotkṣepa*, *lalitākṣepa*, and *krodhākṣepa*—the nine throws (*akṣepas*), the six [movements] beginning with *vajrotkarṣa*, and the twenty-eight gestures (*abhinayas*) for the sword and other weapons.

When performing these thirteen movements, such as the extended right leg and so forth, one should execute, as appropriate: the four modes of stepping—the ocean wave, the mountain-shaking, the playful movement, and the wrathful movement; the nine universal movements; the six [movements] beginning with the raised vajra; and the twenty-eight modes beginning with the sword.

Thereafter, having performed a dance in the *ālīḍha* posture and facing south, one should place the left index finger against the heart, fall to the ground on the left side, and while gazing into the sky, strike down all the Māras with the right hand holding a vajra. This is the "Projection of the Buddha’s Power. (1)

Following that, one should perform a dance with the right leg extended; facing toward the south, holding the left hand in the threatening gesture at the heart, one should fall to the ground on the left side. Looking up into the sky, one should strike all the māras with the right hand together with the vajra—this is the "Universal Stirring by the Power of the Buddha."

Having performed the dance beginning with the *kamalāvarta*, one should raise the vajra and, threatening with the left index finger, lift the *vajradaṇḍamudrā* with the right hand while standing on even feet. With grace, one should step the right foot—bent in the *vajrapada* stance—to a distance of two and a half *tālas*. Keeping the left foot steady, one should place both feet in the position of the wings (*pakṣasthita*). Then, bending the right knee, one should lift up the *daṇḍamudrā*.

Threatening with the left index finger, one should bend down the left abdomen; closing the left eye, one should rotate the face; fixing the gaze upon the mandala, one should knit the brows—this is the "tossing of the unshakable. On the right hip is the withdrawal. (2)

Having performed the dance preceded by the circling of the feet, one should take up the vajra; then, threatening with the left hand in the *tarjanī* (threatening) gesture, one should cast [the vajra] with the right hand in the *daṇḍa-vajra-mudrā*.

Standing in the equal-legged posture (*sama-pāda-sthāna*), one should bend with a haughty vajra-step; having kicked the right leg out two and a half cubits, the left leg is made firm, and the two legs should be positioned like wings. Then, bending the right knee, one should throw [the object] with the staff-mudrā (*daṇḍa-mudrā*).

Having threatened with the left hand in the *tarjani* (threatening) gesture, one should lower the abdomen, close the left eye, turn the face, and look toward the mandala while knitting the brows; this is the "trembling universal movement," which draws [the energy] into the right side of the waist.

In the same way, having raised the *vajra*, standing with feet even, one should extend both feet evenly to a distance of two and a half *tālas* and keep them in a triangular position. Having struck the ground in front, one should raise the *daṇḍamudrā* and gaze [forward]; placing the left index finger on the breast is the "terrifying projection" (*trāsanākṣepa*). The withdrawal is at the region of the left hip. 3.

In that same manner, having raised the vajra and standing in the even-legged posture (*sama-pāda-sthāna*), one should extend the legs evenly to a height of two and a half cubits, forming the feet into a triangle. Having clapped the hands in front, one should cast the staff-mudrā outward;
then, holding the threatening gesture (*tarjanī*) at the left breast, one should cause all who are terrified to tremble and withdraw them toward the left side of the waist.

In the same way, having formed the *vajrotthāna-mudrā* and standing with feet even, one should raise the *daṇḍa-mudrā*, close the right eye, and look at the forefinger on the breast with the left eye. Having placed the left foot in the *vajra-pada* position, bending the right knee and lifting the foot, one should suddenly whirl it to the left like a wheel while displaying wrath. Then, withdrawing that foot, one should place it in the half-*pratyālīḍha* stance, keeping the two feet firm and positioned like wings; this is the *saṃkṣobhaṇākṣepa*.
Through the application of the vajra dance, there is withdrawal at the right hip. || 4 ||

Likewise, having formed the vajra-raising mudrā and standing in the even-legged posture, one should brandish the staff mudrā, close the right eye, and look at the threatening gesture (tarjanī) of the left hand directed toward the breast.
Assuming the vajra-foot stance with the left leg, one should bend the right knee, lift the foot, and while maintaining a wrathful expression, rotate it simultaneously to the left like a wheel.

Again, having drawn back that leg and extended the left, place them in a half-moon posture; the two legs should remain firm like wings. This is the "Perfectly Agitated Universal Movement," and by means of the application of the vajra dance, one should gaze toward the right hip.

Likewise, having performed the *vajrotthāna*, standing with feet even, one should raise the staff-mudrā and look at the forefinger on the breast with the left eye. Contracting the left knee and placing the right in the *vajrapada* stance, one should lift the left and suddenly whirl with the right; then one should set it down. Having made the lowered foot contracted, stationary, and triangular, and having placed the right in the position of a wing, one should stand in the *ālīḍha* posture—this is the *vimohanākṣepa*. While dancing, the withdrawal is performed at the region of the left hip. (5)

Likewise, having raised the vajra and standing in the even-footed posture (*sama-pāda-sthāna*), one should look at the left breast with the left eye while making the staff mudrā (*daṇḍa-mudrā*) and the threatening gesture (*tarjanī*). Bending the left knee and assuming the vajra-step posture (*vajra-pāda-sthāna*) with the right leg, one should throw it to the left and simultaneously circle it to the right.

Then, having set it down and drawn up the leg that had fallen, one should form a triangle; the right [leg] should be positioned like a wing and extended to the right. This is the movement of total delusion (*vibhrama*); having performed the dance, one should contract it toward the left side of the hip.
Or rather, having turned with the left foot, one should again strike with the hand in front and then raise the staff once more; this is specifically the "swift throw" (kṣiprākṣepa). || 6 ||

Having completely circumambulated this very [object] with the left foot, one should again clap the hands in front; furthermore, one should brandish them like a staff—this is the "extraordinarily swift" universal movement.

The "throwing back" (vyāvṛtāsyākṣepa) is indeed a form of "confounding throw" (vimohanākṣepa); however, having opened the mouth and placed the tongue in the manner of licking a bell, one should rotate it like a wheel. || 7 ||

Just as there is an agitation that thoroughly deludes, so too is there an agitation that thoroughly reverses it; nevertheless, with the mouth opened and the tongue positioned like a small bell, one should rotate it like a wheel.

In the same manner, having raised the *vajra* and placed the two feet at a distance of one *tāla*, one should form a triangle. One should slightly bend the right knee and incline the left knee; one should also incline the region of the breast and the left side of the abdomen. Following the tossing of the staff-like arm with the index finger upon the breast, and immediately after casting the gaze upon the staff, the face is whirled around—this is the toss named *Kelīkila*. The withdrawal [of the movement] occurs on the right hip. 8.

Likewise, having raised the vajra and positioned the two feet at a distance of one span, one should form a triangle; the right knee should be slightly bent and the left knee lowered. The breasts and the left side of the abdomen should be pressed down; one should make the threatening gesture (tarjanī) toward the breasts, brandish the staff-like arms, and finally, looking at the staff, strike while turning the face.
*Kilī kilī saṃcodana*: this is the contraction into the right side of the abdomen.

When that very Mahākelīkila has his gaze fixed on the staff and is led behind his own back by means of the region of the right shoulder, with his left eye closed, angry, and taking steps [in a dancing motion], the withdrawal is as before. 9.

This is the great *kilikila*. When looking at the staff while it remains [in place], one should swing the staff from the right side of the shoulder back toward one's own back; then, closing the left eye, one should move the feet about with an expression of wrath. The summary is as before.
Having assumed the left prideful posture, one should raise the vajra at the heart with the right hand; this is the "Vajra-raising" (vajrotkarṣa). || 1 ||
Placing the left hand at the navel and raising the right hand with a vajra at the heart is the "raised vajra" (*vajrotthita*) mudrā.

The *vajrākṣepa* (the vajra-throw) consists of making a threatening gesture at the heart with the index finger raised from the left *vajramuṣṭi*, while performing the manner of striking with a vajra held in the right *vajramuṣṭi*.

[2] The *vajrākṣepa* consists of making a threatening gesture (*tarjanī*) at the heart with the index finger extended from the left *vajramuṣṭi*, while performing the manner of striking with a vajra grasped by the right *vajramuṣṭi*.

The *vajramuṣṭi* (vajra-fist) is formed by pressing the thumbs with the four fingers whose tips are curled together. || 2 || Having extended the hands from the mouth upwards and downwards, one should make the mouth, nostrils, cheeks, and eyes wide open and terrifying; this is the *vajrabhairava* (vajra-terrible). || 3 ||

The vajra-fist (*vajramuṣṭi*) is formed by pressing the thumbs together with the tips of the four fingers firmly clenched. Vajrabhairava is characterized by extending the hands upward and downward from the mouth, while making a threatening gesture with the nostrils, the cheeks, and the eyes.
Having whirled the vajra clockwise with the right hand, he places both feet on the ground in succession; thus he is Vajrakuṇḍalin. || 4 ||
Rotating the vajra in the right hand clockwise and gradually placing both feet upon the ground is the *vajravarta*.
Extending the left arm while holding the base of the right hand—which holds a vajra—at its root, one should dance; this is the Vajra Dance. || 5 ||
Extending the left hand and grasping the base of that [left] hand with the base of the right hand, which holds a vajra, while performing a dance, is the "vajra dance."
Preceded by the vajra-dance, one should tilt the head to the left out of pride; this is the performance of the *strīmāyā* [gesture]. || 6 ||
Preceded by the vajra dance, planting the two heels ten finger-widths apart and bending the head to the left is the performance of the illusion of a woman.

Out of pride, one performs the Vajralāsyā mudrā; drawing the right vajra-fist from the sheath of the left vajra-fist and holding it with the gesture of a sword—this is the sword-gesture (khaḍgābhinaya). || 1 ||

Placing it upon the back is the mudrā of Vajralāsyā. Extending the right index finger from the hollow of the left vajra-fist and drawing it back in the manner of a sword is the sword gesture (khaḍgākāra).
Threatening with the heart, the vajra-gesture consists of the gesture of hurling a three-pronged vajra. || 2 ||
Forming the threatening gesture at the heart and moving it in the manner of brandishing a three-pointed vajra is the vajra method.
The gesture of the pestle (*muṣalābhinaya*) is performed because of the crushing of obstacles with a pestle held in the *vajrabandha* [mudrā]. || 3 ||
Striking the obstructors with the pestle held in a vajra-threatening gesture is the manner of the pestle.

Having formed the *sampuṭāñjali* (the hollowed cupped hands), by joining the tips of the fingers with one another, it becomes the *vajrāñjali*. Likewise, at the base, by binding them together, it is the *vajrabandha*. Having formed the *vajrabandha* of two *vajramuṣṭi*s (vajra-fists) at the heart—having joined the little fingers and the index fingers—one should release them like a wheel; this is the gesture (*abhinaya*) of the wheel.

Binding the palms together and joining the tips of the fingers to one another is the vajra-palms (*vajrāñjali*). Likewise, properly clenching [the hands] at the base is the vajra-clench (*vajramuṣṭi*). When the little fingers and index fingers of two vajra-fists at the heart perform the vajra-clench and rotate like a wheel, it is the manner of the wheel (*cakraprakāra*).
Having gracefully extended the index and middle fingers of the right vajra-fist and holding them upward, this is the *patākā* gesture. || 6 ||
Extending the index and middle fingers of the right vajra-fist while bending them gracefully and holding them upward is the manner of the banner.
One should open the joined palms like a lotus; this is the lotus gesture (*padmābhinaya*). || 7 ||
Joining the palms and opening them like a lotus is the "lotus manner."
Having formed the right fist with the thumb tucked inside, one should extend the index finger and raise the arm upward like a staff; this is the "staff gesture" (daṇḍābhinaya). || 8 ||
Placing the thumb inside the right fist and extending the index finger, raising it above the shoulder like a staff is the *daṇḍa-mudrā* (staff gesture).
One should hold the right index finger with the gesture of drawing [towards oneself]; this is the *aṅkuśa* (goad) gesture. || 9 ||
Holding [the object] by means of the right index finger being hooked is the manner of the iron hook (*aṅkuśa*).
Extending and then contracting the fingers of the right hand constitutes the gesture of the hood (*phaṇābhinaya*). || 10 ||
Extending and then contracting the fingers of the right hand is the manner of the *gdengs ka* (the "swinging" gesture).
Taking the bow with the left hand and drawing the string pressed down by the right hand, one should perform the *vāyudhāraṇa*; this is the dramatic gesture (*abhinaya*) of the bow. || 11 ||
Drawing the cord straight from the left hand to the right up to the ear while holding the breath is the manner of the bow.
One should perform the drawing back of the arrow with the right index and middle fingers at the back; this is the gesture of drawing the arrow (śarākarṣaṇābhinaya). || 12 ||
Drawing the arrow from behind the right index and middle fingers is the manner of drawing the arrow.
From those very two, by means of the gesture of drawing an arrow, there arises the gesture of drawing an arrow. || 13 ||
Next, by the gesture of offering praise, one should place the joined palms (sampuṭāñjali) at the heart; this is the gesture of prostration.
When performing the manner of shooting an arrow with those very same [hands], it is the manner of shooting an arrow.
Having formed two vajra-fists with the tips bent and joined,
one should perform the twisting and unwinding [of the hands], which is the supreme means for summoning the deities.
Having performed the double-vajra binding (*vajrabandha*), one should firmly interlace [the hands] in front. This interlacing and firm interlacing is the supreme for summoning the deities;
thus, through the binding with the *vajrodvalita* mudrā, it is called *vajrodvalita*.
Regarding this, "folding and firmly folding" refers to the firm folding of the vajra, which is performed by binding the mudrā of the firm folding of the vajra.
Some say that, having performed the *vajrodvalita* with the hands below, one should whirl the *vajra* above and move the *vajra* gracefully. 14.
According to some, after performing the vajra-encircling (*vajra-parigraha*), one should circle the vajra and, with a display of pride, cause the vajra to move upward.

The lion’s posture (*siṃhapada*) consists of placing the back of the forearm of the right hand upon the back of the forearm of the left hand, which is extended downward toward one's own mouth. || 15 ||
Facing downward toward one's own face, the left hand is fully extended beneath it, while the right hand is thrust upward behind the back; this is the lion’s posture (*siṃhasthāna*).
Because of looking all around with pride, this very [mudrā] joined with the lolling tongue is the Lion’s Yawn. || 16 ||
One should look about with pride; this very [mudrā], accompanied by the movement of the tongue, is the lion’s yawning smile (*siṃhahasita*).
Having extended the left arm and placed it upon the ground, one should hold the right arm upward in the gesture of dealing a slap with pride; this is the *siṃhākrānta* (lion-trampled) posture.
Pressing the left shoulder down to the ground and striking the cheek with the right hand in the manner of a slap, while maintaining pride directed upward, is the "lion's crouch."
These three should be bound by means of the Vidyādhara-pada. || 17 ||
These three should be bound with the stepping posture of the Vidyādharas.

Standing in the squatting posture (*utkuṭakāsana*), making the gesture of slapping with both hands, forming the *garuḍamudrā* with the tongue, and gazing downward at the *nāgas* with the *vajra-gaze*, one should perform two successive upward tosses; this is the *garuḍāsana*. || 18 ||

Remaining in the squatting posture (*paryaṅka*), one should perform the manner of striking the hands against the cheeks; with the tongue, one should form the *garuḍa-mudrā*, and with the vajra-gaze, one should look downward at the nāgas below, performing one or two movements of it—this is the *garuḍa-posture*.
With the left hand in the vajra-fist gesture at the heart in a threatening pose, and with the right hand making the gesture of whirling a slingshot, there is the *bhindipāla* [mudrā]. 19.
Forming a threatening mudrā with the left hand in the vajra-fist gesture at the heart, while circling the *'ur-rdo* with the right hand, is the ritual of the *'ur-rdo*.
Placing the left hand palm-upward in the lap, with the right hand making the gesture of granting boons, he is Varada (the Giver of Boons). || 20 ||
Placing the left hand in the *paryaṅka* (crossed) position on the shoulder and performing the gesture of supreme generosity (*varada-mudrā*) with the right hand is the "Supreme Generosity" [mudrā].
The gesture of the *śakti* is performed by first raising the left vajra-fist with the threatening finger at the heart, followed by the gesture of hurling a spear with the right hand. || 21 ||

Forming a threatening gesture (*tarjanī*) at the heart with the left vajra-fist while whirling with the right hand as a preliminary, the manner of casting a short javelin is the "short spear" (*kunta*) mudrā.
In the same way, from the gesture of throwing a die, there arises the gesture of a die. || 22 ||
The manner of performing emanations and projections exactly as they are is the manner of the magical tree.
The gesture of the spear is performed by means of the two vajra-fists in the manner of brandishing a spear. || 23 ||
The manner of piercing with a spear using both vajra fists is called the "manner of the spear."

In the directions beginning with the east, having bound the mudrās such as Bodhyagri for Vairocana and the others, there is the empowerment of the four faces through the purity of the four liberations: emptiness, signlessness, wishlessness, and lack of formative activity. || 24 ||

In the directions such as the east, one should consecrate [the site] with the four doors of purification—the emptiness, signlessness, wishlessness, and the unconditioned—by means of the mudrās of supreme enlightenment and so forth, performed by Vairocana and the other [Buddhas].
Having fallen upon the ground with the step of a Vidyādhara, one should perform the gesture of holding a skull-cup and a vajra with the left and right hands; thus is the Vajra-Vidyādhara. || 25 ||
Having fallen upon the ground with the posture of one who holds awareness (*vidyādhara*), the manner of holding a *kapāla* and a vajra with the left and right hands is that of a Vajra-vidyādhara.
In the same manner, by means of his two hands, through the gesture of holding a vajra-garland, he is the bearer of the vajra-garland (Vajramālādhara). || 26 ||
In that very same manner, performing the manner of holding a vajra garland with the hand is "holding a vajra garland."

Having performed the *tāṇḍava* with the right foot, the left foot is placed [on the thigh] in the reverse position; with both hands forming the *vajramuṣṭi*, the two little fingers are linked like a chain (*śṛṅkhalita*), and the two index fingers are made into a needle (*śūcī*). Having turned around, one should hold [the hands] at the head—this is *jālandhara*. The same is done with the left foot as well. 27.

Pressing the right foot against the *tāṇḍava* [stance], one should place the left hand upon the inverted left foot; then, binding both hands in vajra-fists, forming the two little fingers like an iron chain (*śṛṅkhalā*), and turning the tips of the two index fingers inward to grasp at the crown of the head—this is *Jālandhara*.
In the same way, he extends his left leg.
One should place the hands in the *saṃpuṭāñjali* gesture at the heart with the performance of offering praise; this is the performance of salutation. || 28 ||
Placing the palms together at the heart in the manner of one offering praise is the way of prostration.

In the *Śrīhevajra* and other Yoginī Tantras, it is held that the pacification of all obstacles occurs through the mere utterance of the *hūṃ* mantra; thus, no other mantras are taught there. However, in the *Śrīmāyājāla* and other Mahāyoga Tantras, mantras for each of the vajra-words are taught according to their respective degrees [of capacity]. Those [mantras] should be explained right here. Therefore, both [methods] have been stated by us, so that one may perform what is desired.

In the *Śrī Hevajra* and other Yoginī Tantras, it is stated that by the mere recitation of the mantra consisting of the syllable *hūṃ*, all obstacles are pacified; no other mantras are taught therein.

In the Mahāyoga tantras such as the *Śrī-guhyasamāja*, mantras for the vajra foot-steps (*vajrapada*) were taught individually for those who delight in brevity; therefore, those shall also be explained here. Consequently, I shall explain both [the mantras and their application], just as they are to be clearly inscribed.
Namely:
[The first four mantras are given by Mahāmati as derived from oral instruction!
As follows:
Oṃ, O Great Wrathful One with the vajra of the single-pointed staff, shatter, shatter all wicked asuras! Hūṃ phaṭ!
oṃ ae triśūcika vajrapāda mahākrodha bhañja bhañja sarvaduṣṭāsurān hūṃ phaṭ | oṃ triśūcikapadavajramahākrodha bhañja 2 sarvaduṣṭāsurān hūṃ phaṭ ||
oṃ triśūcikapadavajramahākrodha bhañja bhañja sarvaduṣṭāsurān hūṃ phaṭ | oṃ pañcaśūcikapadavajramahākrodha bhañja 2 sarvaduṣṭāsurān hūṃ phaṭ ||

Thereafter, having performed the gesture of salutation (*praṇāmābhinaya*) preceded by the lotus-turning (*kamalāvarta*), one should perform the dance of the cremation-ground dwellers, the lords of the mandala, including the gestures of the cremation ground and their respective pledges (*samaya*). For others, however, there is only the pledge. All of that must be expressed by means of verse alone; performing the gestures according to the meaning of the verses, one should dance.

Thereafter, having performed the manner of prostration and the circumambulation, one should perform the dance in the manner of a charnel ground before the Lord of the Mandala residing in the charnel ground; furthermore, these are the commitments (samaya), and one should perform only the definitive commitments. All of these should be expressed in verse, and the modes of the meaning of the verses should be enacted as a dance.
Furthermore:

Caṇḍogra, terrifying and fearsome, even for the Lord of the Gods, stands upon the back of a directional elephant; he displays the vajra and the threatening gesture, and is perpetually yellow; thereafter comes Vāsuki.
Brilliant white, with seven hoods, a dense cloud, named Caṇḍogra, great, white, possessing fierce and mighty supernatural power, Rājamukha resides upon a Śirīṣa tree in the east. || 1 ||

In the east, the Lord of the Gods (Indra), who is fierce, violent, and terrifying, dwells upon the elephant of the direction; he is always yellow, vividly manifest with a vajra and the threatening gesture (tarjanī). Then there is Vaiśravaṇa, who is white and possesses seven humps; and the great one called Ghanāghana, who is fierce and violent.
Possessing fierce and great miraculous powers, the white elephant-faced one dwells upon the śirīṣa tree.
The Lord of Yakṣas, though situated among the treasures, is yellow, bestows fearlessness, and is equipped with a mace; the Rākṣasa Takṣaka likewise made a "guḍaguḍi" sound in the north.
He was shaken by the glorious Bodhi tree, and this Dambhaka, who has the face of a man, is cool.
The deep abyss is his eternal nourisher; O you whose greatness is profound, the great and terrifying cremation ground is yours. || 2 ||

In the north, the yellow lord of yakṣas is perfectly mounted upon a horse, bestowing fearlessness and holding a staff; likewise, the red Aja is surrounded by a retinue making a "hu-hu" sound. Here, at the glorious Bodhi tree, the one-faced human-faced Śīta stands in full array, his fangs bared.
It is a great charnel ground that causes [all things] to increase as signs, possesses great terror, and is utterly dense and chaotic.
Śukla, who has a tongue as his vehicle and bestows fearlessness, is white; Varuṇa is likewise Viṣṇu, accompanied by a serpent-noose. Karkoṭaka, the lord of serpents, is dark blue.
To the west, a terrible cloud thunders, filled with rising flames.
In Aśoka, he is Makarānana, red in appearance, wearing a hide, and radiant. || 3 ||

In the west is the white Lord of Waters, mounted upon a makara, who brings fearlessness; he holds a great serpent-noose. Likewise, the green nāga, the Lord of the Palms, is the Ocean of Power; he causes deep clouds to thunder. There, completely pervaded by blazing radiance accompanied by joy—
Upon the Ashoka tree, the makara-faced [deity] of an intensely red nature radiates light.
In the southern direction, Kṛṣṇa-Yama always carries a harsh staff and noose;
he is mounted upon a buffalo that is white as a conch shell. Then there is Padma, the lord of the double-tongued serpents, who performs the sprinkling of water daily from his great skull-bowl crest.
Kāla, with a face like that of a fierce, leaping wolf, likewise protected Raṅka.

In the south is Kṛṣṇayama, brandishing a staff of wrath and devoid of a noose; he always rides upon a buffalo. There, the Lord of the two tongues is a most white lotus, who causes the sun to rain down and then withdraw it at each moment. He is a great terror upon the *cūta* tree, possessing the black, wrathful face of a buffalo; thus does the Rākṣasa strike fear.
In the southeast is Dahana, red in color, holding a water-pot (*kamaṇḍalu*) and accompanied by a rosary of mantra-syllables; his elephant is Mahāpadmaka, white as a lotus stalk.
Then there is Ghora, who holds a cloud and has the face of a goat, laughing with a great, boisterous laugh.
Clad in the red branches of the Karañja tree, the naked woman shines with a broad smile.

In the intermediate direction of the Me [southwest], there is one red like fire, holding a *bhiṅgāra* vessel and possessing a mantra rosary; he dwells upon the letter Ra. The Nāga Mahāpadma is white like a lotus stalk; he is the water-holder who strikes fear. Then, the one with a ram’s face (*meṣamukha*) has a great, fierce laugh; he is red and beautiful, dwelling upon the Karañja tree, and possesses a vast, violent laughter.
Kṛṣṇa holds a threatening finger to his head; Sthāṇu is that Nairṛti; Pūraṇa is "wet with moisture"; the serpent Ananta is also blue in form;
and the great one with the face of a bear is "parched, scorched by the heat, and blazing."
Bound by the Nairṛtas, that cremation ground is always filled with loud cries of "kiliki-li."

In the southwest (Nairṛtya) dwells the black Rākṣasa, holding a head and making the threatening gesture; he is of a blue nature, possessing the poison that fills and scatters the moist [world]. He is great, endowed with a black bear-like face, and possesses the *hulu hulu* sound upon the great trees.
It is the perpetual charnel ground where the sounds of the *kai kai li* that truly cause increase resound.
In the northwest dwells Kulika, the lord of great serpents; he blows as the wind, wearing a garment of fine cloth, seated upon a white deer,
cruel, greatly variegated, ever-clouded, greenish-yellow, terrible, and with the face of a deer.
Causing fear to the frightened, he who has resorted to the Arjuna tree shall breathe forth a terrible darkness. || 7 ||

In the northwest is the white Wind Deity, holding a beautiful wind-banner and having the face of a deer; the great lord of the south is Kulika, who is himself the fierce and manifold one. Then there is the one with the face of a great green wild beast, who constantly causes the clouds to revolve.
Terrified and struck with fear, he dwells upon the ṛdhan tree in the unbearable darkness of the charnel ground.
Then there is the grey-colored Īśvara, seated upon a bull and bearing a trident and a skull-cup;
he is closely embraced by Gaurī, wears a great jewel, and is the illustrious Śaṅkhapāla.
Next is Śambhu, manifest with great supernatural power, white in color, bull-faced, and stationed beneath a banyan tree.
And because he is fierce and possesses fierce clouds, he spreads an abundance of splendor through his waters; such is he who is so regarded.

In the northeast is Īśāna, white and yellow, seated upon an elephant and holding a conch and a skull-cup; then there is the glorious Śaṅkhanidhi, with a firm body, white and yellow, holding a great jewel; and Sthāṇu, possessing great supernatural power, white and with the face of an elephant, seated upon a wooden pillar.
The forest of Īśvara is fierce and vast, possessing both great and small ferocity.
When these eight [deities] of fierce radiance, possessing excellent forms, are enraged,
all these directional guardians— serpents marked by seven hoods and having human faces—
as well as the trees laden with flowers and fruit and the mountains blazing with various colors, [are likewise affected].
Upon those trees dwell beings of great supernatural power, namely the Kilikilicakras and the Kauśikas. || 9 ||

In these eight [charnel grounds] possessing the bodies of the eight [lords], within the fierce cremation grounds, all the nāgas—adorned with seven hoods and having human faces—are the leaders of the directions; the trees are laden with flowers and fruit, and the clouds possess various blazing colors.
Just as those trees possess great miraculous power and perform the *kili-kili* [sound], so too does Śakra.

To speak briefly of the manner of the commitments (*samaya*) of those accomplished masters and lords of yoga who reside in cremation grounds:

Lūyipāda, Tilūtī, and Śabara, always holding a staff and a bow in hand, attained perfection even while sleeping and indulging in sensual pleasures with the essence of supreme bliss; likewise, Śāntideva also achieved success.
Vīṇāpāda, however, plays his lute and delights in its resonant, compassionate sound.
The rice-grains strike against the pestle, which is naturally pure and possesses ears for the sake of removing latent impressions.

The soles of his feet cut through all extremes; here at Śavari, he holds a bow and arrow in his hands as signs. He is the deity who accomplishes the desires of those who sleep and eat, endowed with the flavor of supreme bliss. His feet possess the lute, and he utters the sounds of the lute, endowed with the melodic resonance of joy and compassion.
Denghipa is one who threshes grains; Karnapa is one whose mind is naturally pure.
Kuḍḍāladhātrī remains, equalizing the unevenness of the three worlds;
having drunk wine, the deformed one gave even the heat of torment as a pledge to the female liquor-sellers.
But Vyāghrārūḍha, together with his own kinswoman, the Ḍombī, is engaged in an embrace.
Having abandoned both the conceivable and the inconceivable, he who is like Kambalin spreads his woolen blanket over his body.

The Lord who holds the dice is not [bound] by the three realms; having established himself in perfect equanimity, he remains. Virūpākṣa bestows the sun upon the wine-sellers so that they may drink the liquor. Dombipa rides a tiger and is completely embraced by his own consort.
Even the powerful Kamvalī of bliss has utterly lost both thought and non-thought, and his body is fully expanded.
Having enjoyed his desires, Dāriko, impetuous for young women, rejoices; Guṇḍarī swallows a bowstring smeared with sugar; this Guḍḍurika swallows air;
and Indrabhūti, seated upon a lion-throne in the sky, meditates on a kingdom consisting of supreme bliss.
Having gone to Khaḍga through the perfection of the Khaḍga [sādhana], he created for me a garment of light that dispels all weariness.

Dārikapa also desires fine foods and liberation, with the force of delighting in women; Guḍaripa likewise remains in meditative equipoise upon the yogic exercises of the waist, while his breath resounds as "guḍa-guḍi. King Indrabhūti dwells upon a lion throne in the sky, the very nature of the bliss of supreme meditative concentration.
Having ascended into the sky himself, he accomplished the siddhi of the sword; that one of subdued senses was Prabhākara.
This Kṛṣṇa, the protector of the dog-like [devotees], plays with his own bitches like a child; he rejoices in the sky with the sounds of his hand-drum and his consort’s embrace.
Who seeks what purpose when this proclamation resounds everywhere out of compassion?
Thus, this noble Nāgārjuna has benefited the world by bestowing the eight sovereign powers and other such gifts.

Here at the feet of Ku Kuripa, he plays like a child together with his female dogs; Kṛṣṇācārya, having formed a mudrā, fills the sky with the clamor of the *ḍamaru*. When he acts for the sake of anyone whatsoever, he possesses a melodic voice completely encompassed by compassion itself.
He benefits wandering beings by bestowing [attainments] such as the eight great powers of the noble Lord Nāgārjuna and others.
In some places, wise ones sit with affection upon the spread-out corpses; there they eat the *āsali* and drink the *madana*, and prepare the excellent *kunduru*.
They slowly sing of the Lord’s essential principles (*tattva*) in beautiful *vajra-padas*.
These masters of yoga, surrounded by the wheel, roar impetuously.

Some dwell in the various flavorful [realms] with the joy of meditative absorption accompanied by wisdom; they eat great meat, drink intoxicants, and perform the supreme *kunduru* rites. With the vajra-foot posture, they dance in fragments, singing songs endowed with the essence of the *tattva* through their exquisite grace.
These lords of yogins, filled with joy, caused the wheel to revolve evenly with their voices.

The inhabitants of Kāliñjara, who possess the joy of bliss from the union of the *kakkola* and *priyabola*, whose *kundura* trees are radiant, whose hands are like bees for the freshly prepared rice, and who are followers of the Discus-bearer (Viṣṇu),
have their faces like the petals of shining divine lotuses and their lips smeared with [vermilion].
In some places, certain yogins take delight in dwelling in the abodes of hungry ghosts.

With joy, they mix *kakola* with betel; the wheel-bearer (*cakrin*), fortunate and full of delight, has his hands adorned with freshly prepared great meats. The lotus-petal water of the radiant goddesses completely washes away the stains from their teeth. Who are those yogins who, at the site of the abode of flavors, have vowed to experience the taste?
Having placed the intoxicant (*madana*) in a lotus-leaf vessel, they then [add] great rice and various condiments.

The glorious Kāliñjaras, who have not abandoned the true resonance of the sandalwood [mountain], sing at will— some voices modulated by the melodies of the *karpīta* lute, others resting upon their broad chests, all thirsting for the familiarity of the beauty of the *kuṇḍara* drum. And:

Those glorious and fortunate ones who drink liquor placed within vessels of lotus leaves, along with great meat and seasoned condiments, do not abandon their assemblies and possess that which is not the touch of the sublime. Some, relying on the musical lutes resting upon their laps—vessels bound with cords—experience the taste of delight.
Out of his own desire, Śrī Samantaghoṣa, having fully accumulated [merit], sang this melodic hymn.
The entire universe, though ungraspable, always appears as if contained within a mirror;
in that same manner, the mandala-circle, being non-dual, spontaneously transcends the three limits.
Arisen from the union with the Vidyā born of that consciousness, the illustrious one is eternally endowed with the senses.
Homage in every way to that Teacher who, though equal to space, is nonetheless compassionate.

Those various [phenomena] that always reside in the mirror like an ungraspable reflection—likewise, the non-dual maṇḍala-circle is directly perceived as having abandoned the three extremes. Having correctly realized this, one is always glorious and heroic, arising from attachment to the Middle Way.
I bow down to that Teacher who, though equal to the purity of space, is endowed with compassion.
Thereafter, having sat down in the center of the mandala upon a soft and high seat, one should bind the ten seats preceded by the utterance of the syllable *hūṃ*.
Following that, having sat upon a very soft and elevated seat in the center of the mandala, one should bind the ten seats while preceded by the recitation of the syllable *hūṃ*.
Therein, by binding the vajra-paryaṅka and the bhūsparśa mudrās, the vajrāsana [is formed]. || 1 ||
Binding the vajra posture (*vajraparyaṅka*) and the earth-pressing mudrā (*bhūmisparśamudrā*) constitutes the vajra seat (*vajrāsana*).
Meditation arises from the binding of the mudrā of concentration. || 2 ||
Binding the mudrā of meditative concentration is that of dhyāna.
Placing the left foot between the right calf and thigh, and then placing the right foot upon that between the left calf and thigh—this is the vajraparyaṅka posture. || 3 ||
Placing the left foot between the right thigh and calf, and then placing the right foot upon that, between the left thigh and calf, is the vajra-paryanka (vajra posture).
Placing the left leg upon the right leg and bringing the two knees down close together is called the lotus posture (padmāsana). || 4 ||
Placing the left hand upon the right hand with both knees lowered is the lotus seat (*padmāsana*).
Placing the right foot upon the left thigh and placing the left foot upon the surface of the right thigh—this is the sattvaparyaṅka posture. || 5 ||
Placing the right leg upon the left thigh and the left leg beneath the right thigh is the sattvaparyaṅka (heroic posture).
Having assumed the half-lotus posture with the left leg, one should place the right knee upright and straight near it; this is the *vīrāsana*.
Placing the left leg in the half-lotus posture (*ardhaparyaṅka*) and extending the right knee straight close to it is the heroic posture (*vīrāsana*).

Having assumed the half-lotus posture (vāmārdhaparyaṅka) with the right knee resting upon it, one should place the right foot, palm upwards, upon the left thigh; this, some say, is the *vīrāsana*. (6)

Some say that the "heroic posture" (*vīrāsana*) consists of placing the left leg in the half-lotus position (*ardhaparyaṅka*), resting the right knee upon it, and then placing the right foot firmly on the sole of the left thigh.
One seated on a high seat should hold both legs straight; this is the Bhadrāsana posture.
Sitting upon a high seat with both legs held straight is the excellent posture.
Having placed the two feet on the seat with a span's distance between them, one should remain sitting on the heels; this is the utkuṭuka posture.
Placing the two feet on the seat at a distance of one span and remaining with the hands in the lap is the "posture of the seed-vessel" (bīja-puṭa).
Having placed the right foot in the sattvaparyaṅka posture, one should gracefully extend the left; this is the *salīlāsana* (graceful posture). || 9 ||
The *ral-pa’i ’dug-stangs* (the posture of the matted locks) consists of the right leg settled in the *vīrāsana* (heroic posture) and the left leg extended with a slight bend.
Sitting with the two feet joined together is the *svastika* posture. || 10 ||
Standing with the two feet joined together is the "Auspicious" (Bhadra) posture.

Regarding these vajra-postures and so forth, one should gaze forward according to the appropriate application with the two vajra-gazes. It is said that there are two types of gazing: looking directly toward [the object] (*abhimukha*) and looking away from it (*parāṅmukha*). Looking behind (*pṛṣṭhataḥ*) is also mentioned as a form of gazing.

In these [postures], such as the vajra-step (vajrapada) and others, there are likewise vajra-gazes as appropriate; two types of gazes are taught: looking forward is facing toward [the object], and looking backward is facing away.
In this regard, their mantras are as follows:
Oṃ vajrāsana-vajra-mahākrodha pramardaya 2 sarvavighnān hūṃ phaṭ!
Oṃ! O Great Wrathful One, Vajra of the Gesture of Meditation, stabilize 2 all minds! Hūṃ Phaṭ! Oṃ!
O Great Wrathful One, Vajra of the Vajra Posture, destroy 2 all obstacles! Hūṃ Phaṭ! Oṃ!
O Great Wrathful One, Vajra of the Gesture of the Lotus Seat, shatter 2 all enemies! Hūṃ Phaṭ!
Oṃ, O Great Wrathful One of the Vajra Sattvaparyaṅka, threaten, threaten all the great serpents! Hūṃ Phaṭ!
Oṃ, O Great Wrathful One of the Vajra Vīrāsana, destroy, destroy all the wicked ones! Hūṃ Phaṭ!
Oṃ, O Great Wrathful One of the Vajra Bhadrāsanābhinaya, pacify, pacify all sentient beings! Hūṃ Phaṭ!

Oṃ, O Great Wrathful One, Vajra of the squatting posture, squat! Squat! Subjugate all Māras! Hūṃ Phaṭ! Oṃ, O Great Wrathful One, Vajra of the playful posture, cause [them] to enter! Cause [them] to enter! Subjugate all Māras! Hūṃ Phaṭ!
Oṃ, O Vajra Great Wrathful One of the svastika posture, grant well-being! Grant well-being to all sentient beings! Hūṃ Phaṭ!
Oṃ, O Great Wrathful One, Abhimukhavajra, cause all malevolent beings to enter [into a state of possession], hūṃ phaṭ! Oṃ, O Great Wrathful One, Parāṅmukhavajra, turn all obstacles away, hūṃ phaṭ!

oṃ vajrāśana vajramahākrodha pramardaya mardaya sarvavighnān hūṃ phaṭ | oṃ dhyānāśana vajramahākrodha sthiraya sthiraya sarvatrasthāneṣu hūṃ phaṭ | oṃ vajraparyaṅka vajramahākrodha naśaya naśaya sarvavighnān hūṃ phaṭ |

oṃ padmāśānābhaya-vajramahākrodha vidhvaṃsaya sarva śatrūn hūṃ phaṭ | oṃ sattvaparṇakāśāna-vajramahākrodha tarjaya tarjaya sarva mahoragān hūṃ phaṭ | oṃ vīrāśāna-vajramahākrodha trāsaya trāsaya sarva duṣṭān hūṃ phaṭ |

oṃ bhadrāśanahi bhīṇaya vajramahākrodha sugata sugata sugata sarvasattvān hūṃ | oṃ audgukta āśana vajramahākrodha audguktaya audguktaya sarvamārān hūṃ phaṭ | oṃ salīla āśana vajramahākrodha āveśaya āveśaya sarvamārān hūṃ phaṭ |

oṃ svasti kālacakravajramahākrodha kro kro dha svasti svasti sarvasattvānāṃ hūṃ phaṭ | oṃ ābhimukhavajramahākrodha āveśaya sarvaduṣṭān hūṃ phaṭ | oṃ parāṅmukhavajramahākrodha gharaṃ mukhaya paraṃ mukhaya sarvavighnān hūṃ phaṭ | Therein,
these mudrās are to be bound in the vajraparyaṅka posture.
Thereupon, while in the vajra posture, these mudrās should be bound.

As follows: having formed two vajra-fists and making the left hand into a gesture of pride, one should perform the symbolic gesture of holding a vajra with the right hand in the manner of drawing it up to the heart. This is the mudrā of Vajrasattva. (1)

That is to say, having bound the two vajra-fists, placing the left hand at the navel and circling with the right hand at the heart according to the application, the manner of holding the vajra is the mudrā of Vajrasattva.
Placing the left vajra-fist at the heart and extending the index finger, one should grasp it with the right fist; this is for Vairocana. (2)
At the heart, the left hand forms a vajra-fist with the threatening gesture (tarjanī) fully extended, while the right hand grasps it from all sides; this is the mudrā of Vairocana.
Placing the left hand in the lap, one should hold the right hand in the gesture of touching the earth for Akṣobhya. [2 = 3]
Placing the left hand correctly upon the lap and touching the ground with the right hand is the mudrā of Akṣobhya.
In the same way, the right [hand] is in the boon-granting gesture; this is for Ratnasaṃbhava. || 4 ||
Making the supreme gift with the right hand toward suchness belongs to Ratnasambhava.
In the same way, one should hold both hands in the lap in the gesture of meditation for Amitābha.
Binding the right hand at the navel and holding it in the manner of meditative concentration is the mudrā of Amitābha.
In the same way, the right [hand] of Amoghasiddhi is in the gesture of granting fearlessness.
Amoghasiddhi is the one who bestows fearlessness upon reality as it is.
Oṃ vajrasattva hūṃ | Oṃ oṃ | Oṃ hūṃ | Oṃ trāṃ | Oṃ hrīṃ | Oṃ khaṃ | These are, respectively, the mudrās and mantras of Vajrasattva and the others. || ||
oṃ vajrasattva hūṃ | oṃ oṃ oṃ | oṃ hūṃ | oṃ hrāṃ | oṃ hrīḥ | oṃ khaṃ. These are, respectively, the mudrā-mantras of Vajrasattva and the others.

In the lotus posture (*padmāsana*), one should form the *lāsya* and other mudrās. While singing the *hūṃkāra* song, preceded by dance, one should place the two vajra-fists at the waist region on the left and right; thus, with grace, one should slightly incline the head to the left—this is Vajralāsyā.

Upon the lotus seat, one should form the mudrās such as the Graceful One (*lāsyā*). Preceded by the syllable *hūṃ*, the singing of songs, and the performance of dance, one places the two vajra fists of the left and right hands at the region of the hips; then, while arching the body, the head is slightly tilted to the left—this is the Vajralāsyā.
In the same way, from the binding of garlands comes "garland-maker" (*mālākāra*).
Just so, from the binding of garlands comes "garland-maker."

With the index finger of her left hand raised like a staff from a vajra-fist, and with the index finger of her right hand in a dancing gesture, she should play the lute while singing; thus she is the *Gītā*.

With the index finger of her left hand held like a staff from a vajra-fist, and making a dancing motion with the index finger of her right hand, she sings while moving gracefully and swaying; this is the *Gītā* who plays the vīṇā.

Having whirled with both hands and released them from the two sides, and being full of passion and joy while positioned at the head through the application of dance—this is the *nṛtyā* (dancing) mudrā.

{75b4} Having rotated with both hands and released them, having whirled around the two sides, and with grace and exhilaration, performing the application of dance at the position of the crown of the head—this is the dancing [mudrā].
In that regard, their mudrās and mantras are as follows: Oṃ vajralāsye hūṃ | Oṃ vajramāle hūṃ | Oṃ vajragīte hūṃ | Oṃ vajranṛtye hūṃ || |||1||
The mantras for the mudrās are as follows: Oṃ vajralāsyai hūṃ; Oṃ vajramāle hūṃ; Oṃ vajragīte hūṃ; Oṃ vajranṛtyai hūṃ.
With the sattvaparyaṅka posture, [these are for] Vajrasattva and the other Bodhisattvas.
In the bodhisattva’s cross-legged posture are Vajrasattva and the other bodhisattvas;
[the goddess] Sagarvotkarṣaṇī stands with two [hands] holding a goad,
and Sādhukārā stands at the heart through the yoga of drawing back an arrow.
The one with the heart draws [the object] in; both remain holding the iron hook. The application of drawing the arrow is performed well, abiding at the heart.
In the consecration, however, there is the display of the double-vajra at the heart and the sun;
likewise, the staff-like arm situated on the left is turned toward the mouth.
The empowerment of the two vajras, the extraction of the sun into the heart, the staff in the left armpit, and likewise the complete circling around the face.
Blossoming to the right and left, with the heart on the left, she is the slayer with the sword;
whirled like a circle of fire, she issues from the two mouths of the vajra.
With the right and left [hands] fully extended, the application of the left hand at the heart, and the well-performed [gesture] abiding at the chest, one should raise the two vajras toward the face.
The Vajra-dance is free from the whirling motion; the Kapota-mudrā is positioned at the uṣṇīṣa;
the armor-mudrā has its little fingers and tips of the fangs pressed together by the two fists.
The vajra-encircled [mudrā] is formed by releasing the palms at the crown of the head; the armor [mudrā] is formed by the tips of the little fingers; and the two fists are firmly clenched.

"By means of the *vīrāsana* [hero’s posture] and the mudrās of Vajrakrodha and the others" means:

having formed fists with both hands, with the middle fingers like needles and the ring fingers likewise positioned in the *vajrabandha*, one binds the two index fingers in the shape of an earring; then, the two thumbs, situated at the mouth, should be slightly bent in a curved shape—this is for Yamāntaka.

Forming fists with both hands, the tips of the middle fingers and the ring fingers likewise remain in the vajra-fearful posture; the two index fingers are bound in the manner of a coil, slightly bent and directed toward the thumbs—this is the mudrā of Yamāntaka.
Placing the left wrathful fist at the heart, one should raise the right hand in the form of a slap; this is the mudrā of Aparājita.
Placing the left wrathful fist at the heart, raising the right hand in the manner of striking the cheek is the [mudrā] of Aparājita.

Forming the vajra-fist with both hands, binding the two little fingers into a chain-knot, and joining the tips of the two index fingers like a needle, one should rotate them and hold them at the forehead; this is the [mudrā] of Hayagrīva.

Pressing the nails of the little fingers with the two thumbs, one should hold the remaining fingers, characterized by the vajra, at the base of the armpits with the "vajra-binding of the arms" (*bāhuvajrabandha*); this is the *amṛtakuṇḍalī* [mudrā].
Oṃ Yamāntaka hūṃ | Oṃ Prajñāntaka hūṃ | Oṃ Padmāntaka hūṃ | Oṃ Amṛtakuṇḍalivighnāntaka hūṃ. These are the mudrās and mantras of Yamāri and the others. || 0 ||
oṃ yamāntakṛta hūṃ | oṃ prajñāntakṛta hūṃ | oṃ padmāntakṛta hūṃ | oṃ amṛtakuṇḍali vighnāntakṛta hūṃ | These are the mudrā-mantras of Yamāntaka and the others.

Regarding the *bhadrāsana* (auspicious posture), it is the mudrā of Maitreya and the others. Having formed two vajra-fists, one should hold the index fingers, thumbs, and middle fingers of each hand facing one another like *nāgakeśara* flowers; this is the mudrā of Maitreya.
Having bound both vajra-fists, holding them like a *nāgakeśara* flower by bringing the index fingers, thumbs, and middle fingers of each hand toward one another, this is the mudrā of Maitreya.

Having joined the palms together in the *saṃpuṭāñjali* gesture, one should hold them in the shape of a blooming blue lotus by pressing the tips of the two index fingers against the nails of the two ring fingers; this is the mudrā of Mañjuśrī.
Having placed the left hand palm-upward in the lap, one should perform the gesture of an elephant’s trunk with the right hand extended;
this is the [mudrā] of Gandhahastin.
Raising the left vajra-fist upward, one should lower the right hand beneath it in the gesture of holding a banner; this is for Jñānaketu.
Raising the left vajra-fist upward and lowering the right hand beneath it in the manner of holding a banner is for Jñānaketu.
Having formed the *saṃpuṭa-añjali* mudrā, one should hold it at the heart; this belongs to Bhadrapāla.
The palms joined together at the heart belong to Bhadrapāla.
One should perform the gesture of drawing in waves with all the fingers of both hands fully extended; this is the mudrā of Sāgaramati.
Placing the left vajra-fist at the heart, one should make the right hand in the gesture of granting boons (*varada*). This is [the mudrā] of Akṣayamati.
Placing the left vajra-fist upon the lap and forming a vajra-fist with the right hand, one should snap the thumb and forefinger;
this is the mudrā of Pratibhānakūṭa.
One should perform the gesture of a slightly blossomed lotus with both hands; this is the mudrā of Mahāsthāmaprāpta.

One should perform the gesture of casting away evil with both hands for Sarvāpāyajaha. One should perform the gesture of striking with both hands joined in a hollowed cup for Sarvaśokatamonirghātamati.
One should perform the gesture of flames with both hands extended for Jvālinīprabha.
The manner of vigorously brandishing two scorpions with both hands [... is that of the Jālinī.
For Candraprabha, one should extend the thumb and index finger of the left vajra-fist sideways from the right hand, which is in the *varada* gesture, in the manner of the moon. 13.

With the right hand in the gesture of supreme generosity (*varada-mudrā*), and the left hand in a vajra-fist with the index finger and thumb extended to form the shape of a crescent moon, this is the [mudrā] of Candraprabha.
Having performed the mudrā of the water-pot with both hands, one should hold it at the place of consecration for Amitaprabha.
Holding [the vessel] at the place of empowerment with both hands in the manner of a vase is that of Amitābha.
Having formed the left vajra-fist and, by means of yoga, having shifted it to the right, one should whirl the right vajra-fist in the sky; this is the mudrā of Gaganagañja. 15.
Placing the left vajra-fist in a proud manner upon the back and circling the right vajra-fist in the sky is the [mudrā] of Gaganagañja.

Placing the left hand in the gesture of touching the earth (bhūsparśa), one should hold the index finger and thumb of the right vajra-fist together in the manner of a question mark; this is the mudrā of Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin. 16.

Having established the manner of touching with the left hand, one holds it in the form of an inquiry by joining the index finger and thumb of the right vajra-fist; this is the mudrā of Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin.
