oṃ mīḥ | oṃ muḥ | oṃ gandhahastine hūṃ | oṃ jñānaketujñānavati hūṃ | oṃ bhadravati bhadrāpāle hūṃ | oṃ śākare mahāśākare hūṃ | oṃ kṣaye hūṃ | akṣayakarmāvaraṇapariśodhane svāhā | oṃ pratebhāne pratibhānakūṭe hūṃ | oṃ sthame mayhāsthāmarati svāhā |

oṃ sarvābhayadite sarvāpāyaviśodhani hūṃ | oṃ sarvaśokatamonirghātanamate hūṃ | oṃ jvalini mahājvālini hūṃ | oṃ candre candravatī lokini te svāhā | oṃ amitaprabhe amitamate hūṃ | oṃ gagane gaganaparalokini hūṃ | oṃ sarvanivaraṇaviṣkambhini hūṃ ||
This refers to the mantras of the mudrās of loving-kindness and the others, according to their respective order.

In the squatting posture (*utkuṭukāsana*), the mudrās of the male and female messengers (*dūta-dūtī*) and the male and female servants (*ceṭa-ceṭī*) are to be bound. By binding the two vajra-fists with the index fingers as hooks (*aṅkuśa*), there is the Great Hook (*mahāṅkuśī*) at the little fingers. With the arms crossed and the thumbs pressing against the backs [of the hands], [the mudrās are formed]. *Oṃ vajrāṅkuśa hūṃ jaḥ | Oṃ vajrasphoṭa hūṃ vaṃ | Oṃ vajrāveśa hūṃ hoḥ |* These are the mantras for the mudrās of the Messenger Vajra-Hook and the others.

Having formed the hook with the index fingers of two vajra-fists, one should join the little fingers as a great hook, the palms [of the fists] as a knot, and the tips and backs of the curved knives. *Oṃ vajrāṅkuśa hūṃ jaḥ | oṃ vajrapāśa hūṃ hūṃ | oṃ vajrasphoṭa hūṃ vaṃ | oṃ vajrāveśa hūṃ hoḥ*—these are the mudrā-mantras of the Vajrāṅkuśa and the others.

Having formed the *saṃpuṭa-añjali* (the hollowed-cupped palms), one should place the two index fingers and middle fingers in the shape of an earring upon the middle joints; then, one should hold the two thumbs at the base of the sides of the index fingers. This is the mudrā of Cundā.
Having joined the palms together, placing the joints of the index and middle fingers in the form of a ring, and holding the thumb at the base of the side of the index finger is the *Cundā* [mudrā].
Having formed the vajra-bind, one should hold the two index fingers joined together and the two thumbs in the shape of a jewel upon the head; this is the mudrā of Ratnolkā.
Having formed the vajra-bond, one should join the two index fingers and extend them, holding the two thumbs above in the form of a jewel; this is the mudrā of Ratnatārā.

Having formed the añjali mudrā by extending both hands, one should cover the inner nail of the little finger with the two thumbs, and hold the remaining fingers together like a needle, slightly apart. This is the mudrā of Bhṛkuṭī.

Having fully extended both hands and joined them in *añjali*, one should cover the nails of the two little fingers with the thumbs, while the remaining fingers are each brought together at their tips; this is the *grahaṇa* (seizing) mudrā of Bhṛkuṭī.
Having formed a vajra-fist with each of the two hands separately, one should bind a chain with the little fingers and the index fingers. This is the mudrā of Vajraśṛṅkhalā.

Extending each of the two hands individually, one forms vajra-fists; then, binding the little fingers and index fingers together like an iron chain and carrying them [in front], this is the mudrā of Vajraśṛṅkhalā.
Oṃ cale cule cunde svāhā | Oṃ ratnolkā ratnajvālinī svāhā | Oṃ bhṛkuṭi hūṃ | Oṃ vajraśṛṅkhale hūṃ phaṭ svāhā. These are the mantras of the messenger mudrās.
oṃ cale cule cuṇḍe svāhā | oṃ ratnoṣṇīṣe ratnavyūhini svāhā | oṃ bhrīḥ kūṭi bhrīḥ svāhā | oṃ vajraśṛṅkhale hūṃ phaṭ svāhā | These are the mantra-seals of the female messengers.

Extending both hands, one should press the nails of the left little finger and ring finger with the right thumb; then, inserting the middle and index fingers of the right hand into the center of the left hand, one should hold it at the heart. Having drawn the right hand out from the sheath of the left fist with a gesture of drawing, one should hold it with a sword-gesture. This is the [mudrā] of Ākarṣācala.

With both hands fully extended, one presses the nails of the little finger and the ring finger with the thumbs; placing the middle and index fingers of the right hand upon the center of the left hand and holding them at the heart, one draws and grasps as if drawing a sword from within the hollow of the left fist—this is the Acala [mudrā].
Having joined the two vajra-fists back-to-back with one another, one should form a noose by interlocking the little fingers and extending the two index fingers; this is the mudrā of Ṭakkirāja.
Joining the two vajra fists back-to-back, binding the little fingers like an iron chain and fully extending the index fingers to form a noose is the mudrā of Kāmarāja.
Having placed the two fingers of the left wrathful hand at the heart, one should hold the fingers of the right wrathful hand upright in the form of a staff; this is the [mudrā] of Nīladaṇḍa.

Placing the fingers of the left hand in the wrathful gesture at the heart, one raises and grasps [the staff] with the right hand in the form of a wrathful fist making the motion of a club; this is the Blue Club (Nīladaṇḍa).
Placing the left vajra-fist at the heart, one should raise the right vajra-fist in the gesture of a blow; this is for Mahābala.
Raising [the hand] by means of striking with the vajra-fist gesture placed at the heart with the left vajra-fist is the [mudrā] of Mahābala.
The mudrā of Ṭakkirāja consists of two raised index fingers; that of Sumbharāja is the same.
The mudrā of the King of Desire is like [the previous], but with the two index fingers extended; this is the mudrā of the King Ghaṇṭākarṇa.

Having linked the little fingers and thumbs of both hands together like a chain, one should extend the remaining fingers in the shape of a half-tripatāka. With a forceful utterance of "HŪṂ," this is the mudrā of Vajrapātāla.

Having joined the little fingers and thumbs of both hands together like an iron chain, and having extended the remaining fingers upward in the manner of three banners with a swaying motion while uttering "HŪṂ," this is the Vajra Pātāla mudrā.

These are the seed-syllables of the mantras for those servants: Oṃ acala hūṃ hāṃ | Oṃ ṭakki hūṃ jaḥ | Oṃ nīladaṇḍa mahābala hūṃ | Oṃ krodha hūṃ jaḥ | Oṃ sumbha nisumbha hūṃ | Oṃ gṛhṇa 2 hūṃ | Oṃ gṛhṇāpaya 2 hūṃ | Oṃ ānaya ho bhagavan vidyārāja hūṃ phaṭ | Oṃ vajrapātāla bhañja 2 hūṃ |

The words of the mudrā-mantras for those wrathful ones are as follows: Oṃ ācala hūṃ hūṃ | Oṃ takki hūṃ jaḥ | Oṃ nīladaṇḍa mahādaṇḍa hūṃ | Oṃ krodha jūṃ jaḥ | Oṃ sumbha ni sumbha hūṃ | gṛhṇa gṛhṇa hūṃ | gṛhṇāpaya gṛhṇāpaya hūṃ | ānaya ho bhagavān vidyarāja hūṃ phaṭ | Oṃ vajrapātāla bhanda bhanda hūṃ ||
Preceded by the *kamalāvarta* dance, one should place the *vajrāñjali* at the head, lower it to the heart, and perform the gesture of offering flowers. This is for the goddess Puṣpā.
Preceded by the dance of the *pad-kor*, one should join the vajra-palms at the crown of the head and bring them to the heart; performing the manner of offering flowers is the rite of Puṣpā.

In the same manner, forming the two vajra-fists with the middle fingers raised and touching each other's backs, one should rotate the hand while performing the gesture of offering incense; this is the mudrā of Dhūpā.

In that same manner, with the two vajra-fists turned back-to-back, one should grasp the middle fingers and perform the gesture of offering incense; rotating the hands is the mudrā of the incense goddess.
In the same manner, having raised the two thumbs from the vajra-bind, one should rotate the hand while performing the gesture of offering a lamp; this is for Dīpā.

In that same manner, one should raise both thumbs from the vajra-fearful gesture (*vajrabhairava-mudrā*) and perform the ritual of offering illumination; this is the dance-circumambulation of the *Snang gsal ma*.

Having formed the *talavajrabandha* (the thunderbolt-bind of the palms), having coiled the two thumbs, having extended the two little fingers and joined them at their tips, and having rotated [them] while enacting the gesture of offering perfume; then, preceded by dance, by means of both hands, from the act of smearing—this is for *Gandhā*.

Displaying the palms of the vajra-bond (*vajrabandha*), making the thumbs like a ring, and joining the tips of the fully extended little fingers while circling them completely—preceded by a dance in the manner of offering scented water—the two hands should apply the ointment; this is the "human scent-water."
And these are the mudrā-mantra syllables of those female attendants: Oṃ vajrapuṣpe hūṃ | Oṃ vajradhūpe hūṃ | Oṃ vajradīpe hūṃ | Oṃ vajragandhe hūṃ.
The mantra words for the mudrās of those female servants are as follows: Oṃ vajrapuṣpe hūṃ; Oṃ vajradhūpe hūṃ; Oṃ vajradīpe hūṃ; Oṃ vajragandhe hūṃ.

Regarding the "mudrā of the World Protectors and others in the playful posture" (lalitāsanena lokapālāmudreti): one should perform the mudrās of the World Protectors and so forth while in the playful sitting posture.
Displaying the vajra with the left hand and holding the vajra of the right hand at the waist, one should show it; this is for Śakra.
Having correctly displayed the vajra of the left hand, one holds the vajra of the right hand at the region of the hips; this display belongs to Śakra.

Having bent the right index finger in the shape of a coil and held it at the third joint of the needle-like middle finger, one should display the three [fingers]—the thumb and the sides of the index finger—to the fire.

Drawing back the right index finger in the shape of a hearth and grasping it at the third joint of the middle finger, with the thumb resting against the side of the index finger—this is the mudrā of the Fire Deity.

Having placed the two hands facing each other, with the pair of backs joined within the vajra-bind, one should form a needle with the ring fingers on the outside and hold it at the heart; this is for Yama.

Placing the two hands in a threatening *vajra* gesture with the palms facing inward, one forms the tips of the two thumbs on the inside and the tips of the two ring fingers on the outside, holding them at the heart; this is the [mudrā] of Yama.
Having formed a fist with the right hand and bent the middle and index fingers, one should hold the left hand at the hip region in the shape of a sword. This is for Nairṛti.
Forming a fist with the right hand, with the middle and index fingers bent, and holding the left hand at the region of the hip as if grasping a drawn sword is the mudrā of Nairṛti.
One should join the index finger and thumb of the right hand together; this is the noose mudrā (pāśamudrā) of Varuṇa.
Joining the index finger and thumb of the right hand while holding the left hand in a fist at the heart is the *pāśa-mudrā* of Varuṇa.

With the left fist, one should join the middle finger with the needle-point [of the right hand] and fix the index finger at the third joint in the shape of an earring, extending it forward; having placed the right hand on the region of the hip, one should display this mudrā of Vāyu.

Holding the left fist at the third joint with the middle finger extended and the index finger curled, and extending it forward, one places the right hand upon the region of the hip; this is the mudrā of the Wind Deity.

Having brought the two hands together facing each other, one should form the inner vajra-bind with the two little fingers like a needle, and behind that, one should hold the pair of ring fingers separately. This is for Kuvera.
Forming the vajra-fear gesture with both hands directed inward, and then joining the tips of the two little fingers to the respective ring fingers behind them, is that of Virūpākṣa.

Joining both hands together to form the añjali, one should perform the *talavajrabandha* with the ring fingers; the pair of thumbs should rest upon the middle fingers. One should hold the two index fingers in the shape of a vajra, with the middle fingers acting as the point. This is for Īśāna.

Join the two hands together in the añjali gesture; place the ring fingers and little fingers within the palms in a threatening vajra posture, and resting the two thumbs upon the middle fingers, draw the tips of the middle fingers toward each other with the two index fingers in the form of a vajra and hold them—this is the mudrā of Īśāna.
Holding the two hands in the form of a hollowed añjali mudrā and gazing upward, [this is the gesture] for Brahmā and the other deities.
Holding [the hands] correctly in the manner of palms joined and looking upward is the [mudrā] of Brahmā and the others.
Joining the two hands together, with the tips of the fingers interlaced, and placing the thumbs in a circular shape while looking downward—this is the mudrā of Earth and the other elements.

Joining the two hands together and separating them, with the tips of the fingers joined to one another, one should form the shape of rounded thumbs and gaze downward; this is the mudrā of the Earth Goddess and the others.
Then the words of the mudrā-mantra are as follows:
*Namo vajrāsya diśi diśi vajrapāṇe rakṣa 2 svāhā*.
O Agni, come, come! O Kapilā-kapila, blaze, blaze! Phaḥ phaḥ! O peacock-feathered one, O Virūpākṣa, svāhā!
To Yama, svāhā!
O terrifier of all beings, act, act! Svāhā!
*tṛbhṛpuṭa tṛbhṛśikhi toli virūpākṣa svāhā | oṃ svasakhākhakhṛkhaḥ svāhā | oṃ kuverāya svāhā |*
Oṃ jyūṃ 2 śiva svāhā.
Thus end the mudrās and mantras of the eight [deities] beginning with Śakra.
Namaḥ vajrāya śide śide vajrapāṇe rakṣa rakṣa svāhā | Oṃ āgne ehyehi kapila āyāhi kapila jvala āyāhi jvala haha śikhitoḷi virūpa ākṣa svāhā | Oṃ yamāya svāhā | Oṃ sarvabhūtavyaṅkara kuru kuru svāhā |

oṃ tri tri pu ṭa dri dri śi khi to li bi r’u pa ākṣa svāhā | oṃ su sa kh’a kha khu khaḥ svāhā | oṃ ku bee r’a ya svāhā | oṃ śdzhuṃ śdzhuṃ śi ba svāhā | These are the mudrā-mantras of the eight [deities] beginning with Śakra.
To Brahman above, svāhā!
To Sūrya, lord of the planets, svāhā!
To Candra, lord of the lunar mansions, svāhā!
Thus end the mudrās and mantras of Brahmā and the others.
oṃ āu ṛṅga prātmane svāhā | oṃ sūryagrahādhipataye svāhā | oṃ candranakṣatrādhipataye svāhā | These are the mudrā-mantras of Brahmā and the others.
Then: Svāhā to the Earth!
Svāhā to the Asuras!
"To the Nāgas, svāhā!"—
thus are the mudrās and mantras for Earth and the others.
oṃ āḥ dhvāḥ pṛthivīyai svāhā | oṃ āḥ surebhyaḥ svāhā | oṃ nāgebhyaḥ svāhā | These are the mudrā-mantras of the Earth Goddess and the others.
Thus, the seats, mudrās, and mantra-words spoken in the *Māyājāla*, which are common to all maṇḍalas, must certainly be bound [in practice]. ||o||
Thus, it is taught in the *Māyājāla*: by means of the common postures, mudrās, and mantra-words for all maṇḍalas, the very certainty [of the practice] is bound.

Then, having sprinkled the mandala ground with scented water and having worshipped it with flowers, incense, and so forth, as well as with incense burners and the like at the four corners and four gates, and with dance and song; and having touched it with his hand, recited one hundred and eight times the mantra of the Lord of the Mandala and the hundred-syllable mantra seven times; and while emanating and reabsorbing the circle of deities right there, he should lie down.

Then, having sprinkled the ground of the maṇḍala with scented water, and having properly worshipped it with flowers, incense, and so forth, as well as with incense burners at the four corners and the four gates, and with dance, song, and so on; and having touched it with one's hand and recited the mantra of the Lord of the Maṇḍala one hundred and eight times and the hundred-syllable mantra seven times; one should go to sleep right there while emanating and reabsorbing the wheel of deities.
This is the ritual for the appropriation of the site (*bhūmiparigrahavidhi*).
Thus ends the ritual for the complete appropriation of the earth.
